note.text:
A line segment [AB] is the part of a line between A and B. Its length is written AB, without brackets.

The midpoint M of [AB] is the point of [AB] that is at the same distance from A and from B.

Midpoint property: if M is the midpoint of [AB], then M is on [AB] and AM = MB = AB ÷ 2. For example, if AB = 10 cm, then AM = MB = 5 cm.

Converse: if M is on [AB] and AM = MB, then M is the midpoint of [AB].

Be careful: both conditions are needed. A point can be at the same distance from A and from B without being on [AB]. Then it is not the midpoint.

To find the midpoint with a ruler: measure AB, divide by 2, and mark that length from A.

worked_example.problem: On a ruler, A is at the {a} cm mark and B is at the {b} cm mark. At which mark is the midpoint M of [AB], and what is AM?
steps: AM = AB ÷ {two} = {b - a} ÷ {two} = {(b - a) / two} cm.
M is {(b - a) / two} cm after A: {a} + {(b - a) / two} = {a + (b - a) / two}, so M is at the {a + (b - a) / two} cm mark.
Check: MB = {b} − {a + (b - a) / two} = {b - (a + (b - a) / two)} cm, which equals AM.
worked_example.answer: M is at the {a + (b - a) / two} cm mark, and AM = {(b - a) / two} cm.

cards.idea: On a ruler, the length of a segment is the difference between its two marks.
example: A is at {a} cm and B is at {b} cm.

check.prompt: On a ruler, A is at the {a} cm mark and B is at the {b} cm mark. Find AB.

misconceptions.explain: The length is the difference between the marks: {b} − {a}.

cards.idea: The midpoint M of [AB] is the point of [AB] exactly in the middle: AM = MB = AB ÷ {2}.
example: AB = {d} cm, so AM = MB = {d} ÷ {two} = {d / two} cm.

cards.idea: Converse: if M is on [AB] and AM = MB, then M is the midpoint. Both conditions are needed: a point away from [AB] can also have MA = MB.
example: M on [AB] and AM = MB → M is the midpoint.
MA = MB but M not on [AB] → M is not the midpoint.

pick.text: M is on [AB] and AM = MB.
MA = MB, but M is not on [AB].

misconceptions.explain: M is the midpoint only when it is on [AB] AND AM = MB.

solution: The midpoint needs both: M on [AB] AND AM = MB.

questions.prompt: M is the midpoint of [AB] and AB = {d} cm. Find AM.

misconceptions.explain: M is in the middle, so AM is half of AB: {d} ÷ 2.
AM is part of AB, so it is shorter than AB: {d} ÷ 2.

solution: M is the midpoint, so AM = AB ÷ {2}.

questions.prompt: M is the midpoint of [AB] and MB = {x} cm. Find AB.

misconceptions.explain: MB is only half of AB. AB = AM + MB = {x} + {x}.
AB is the whole segment, so it is longer than MB: AB = 2 × {x}.

solution: MB is half of AB, so AB = {2} × MB.

questions.prompt: On a ruler, A is at the {a} cm mark and B is at the {b} cm mark. At which mark is the midpoint of [AB]?

misconceptions.explain: {(b - a) / 2} cm is the length AM. The midpoint is {(b - a) / 2} cm after A: {a} + {(b - a) / 2}.
Start from A's mark, not from 0: {a} + {(b - a) / 2}.

solution: AB = {b} − {a} = {b - a} cm, and half of it is {(b - a) / 2} cm.
The midpoint is {(b - a) / 2} cm after A: {a} + {(b - a) / 2} = {(a + b) / 2}.

questions.prompt: MA = MB = {x} cm. Can you be sure that M is the midpoint of [AB]?
questions.correct: No: M must also be on [AB].

distractors.text: Yes, because {x} is a whole number.
No: the midpoint is never at the same distance from A and B.

misconceptions.explain: Many points are at the same distance from A and B (all the points of the perpendicular bisector). Only the one on [AB] is the midpoint.
The size of the number does not matter. Check whether M is on [AB].
The midpoint is always at the same distance from A and B. But being at the same distance is not enough on its own.

solution: Every point of the perpendicular bisector of [AB] has MA = MB, but only one of them is on [AB].

questions.prompt: M is the midpoint of [AB] and AB = {d} cm. One statement is false. Which one?

wrong.explain: AM is half of AB: {d / 2} cm.
AM is half of AB, not double: {d / 2} cm.
AM + MB is the whole segment: {d} cm.
